unit.title: Undertake fabrication, forming, bending and shaping – (basic)

summary: This Level 3 unit teaches you the basics of forming, bending and shaping metal in a fabrication shop. You will learn to plan a forming job, work out blank sizes and other sums, use press brakes, folders, rolls and benders safely, allow for springback and material behaviour, roll cylinders and rings, bend pipe and sections, hot form bar, inspect formed parts, investigate faults and supervise others.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). It covers the basics of **fabrication, forming, bending and shaping**: planning a forming job, working out blank sizes, bending sheet and plate on a press brake or folder, rolling cylinders and rings, bending pipe, tube and sections, hot forming bar, inspecting formed parts, and leading others safely on forming machines.

At Level 3 you are expected to plan the work and do the sums yourself, choose the machine and tooling, explain why parts spring back, crack or come out the wrong size, check first-off and batch parts against the drawing, and supervise trainees on machines that can crush or draw in a hand in a moment.
**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 3 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust centres and other providers, and fabricators who make brackets, channels, tanks, gutters, handrails, gates and frames.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Plan the job
Read the drawing and process sheet; work out blank sizes and a cutting list; plan the bending order; make and check a first-off.
Use forming machines safely
Check guards, light curtains, two-hand controls and emergency stops; isolate and lock off for tool changes; control sheet whip and nip points.
Understand how metal bends
Explain the neutral axis, springback, thinning, work hardening, grain direction and the effect of temperature.
Do the calculations
Bend allowance and deduction, blank lengths, die openings, bending force, cylinder and ring lengths, arc lengths, weights, output and out-of-roundness.
Bend on a press brake or folder
Choose tooling, set the back gauge, air bend or bottom, allow for springback, use relief cuts.
Roll plate and sections
Pre-bend, roll in steps with a template, avoid peaking and coning, roll angle and flat bar into rings.
Bend pipe and sections; hot form bar
Choose the radius and method; notch angle for corners; heat to the right colour; avoid burning and blue-heat cracking.
Inspect and report
Measure angles, radii, flanges and flatness; tag rejects; investigate faults; keep the job card.
Supervise others
Train, watch and correct team members, and stop unsafe work.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on planning, machine safety, materials, calculations, press brake work, rolling, pipe and section bending, hot forming, inspection, supervision and records.

A **written paper**: short answers that need exact terms (for example crowning, K-factor, scale, normalising, protractor, two-hand control, lockout, blade clearance, hold-down) and essays in full sentences, with any sums worked out.

**Practical tasks** done as a group: planning and forming a batch of channel brackets with first-off and batch inspection; and rolling, tacking and inspecting a cylinder with a formed end ring, with a quality report.

blocks.note: Show your working in every sum: write the formula, put in the numbers with their units, and check the answer against common sense. A blank longer than the sum of the outside sizes of a bent part is a sign you added instead of took away.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Read the drawing and the process sheet

blocks.p: The **drawing** gives the material, thickness, sizes, bend angles, inside radii and tolerances. The **job or process sheet** gives the order of operations, the machine and tooling, and the checks. Check the material in stock matches the drawing (grade, temper, thickness) before you cut anything.

flow: Work out the blank size (from bend allowance, bend deduction or the shop's bend chart) and show the working
Write a cutting list: blanks for the batch plus one or two spares for setting up
Choose the machine and tooling; check the force needed is within the machine's and the tools' ratings
Plan the **bending order**, so earlier flanges do not foul the tools or the machine on later bends
Cut and deburr the blanks; mark bend lines where needed (with a pencil or soapstone, not a scriber, on the outside of a bend: a scratch can start a crack)
Set the back gauge and bend a **first-off** part
Check the first-off fully against the drawing; adjust and repeat until it passes; sign it off and keep it as the sample
Run the batch, checking parts at set intervals (for example every fifth part)
Record settings, results and rejects on the job card

blocks.p: A first-off proves the blank size, the tooling and the machine settings are right **before** the rest of the batch is made. Bending 50 parts and then finding the flange is 3 mm short wastes all 50.

ul: Bend from the outside in on boxes and trays, so that early flanges point away from the tools on later bends.
Make the bends that need the back gauge against a straight, uncut edge first.
On a box with four sides, check that the last bends can be made without the part hitting the top tool or the machine frame; a box-and-pan folder with removable fingers helps.
Draw the sequence on the process sheet so the next operator does it the same way.
Use the **back gauge** (or a stop) so every bend is the same distance from the edge; check it on the first part.
Bend against the same reference edge on every part.
Keep blanks the same: cut from the same sheet, with the grain in the same direction where it matters.

blocks.p: If the customer asks for a change after the job has started (for example a different bend angle), get it **in writing** and have the drawing revised before changing anything. Mark which parts were made to which revision.

Forming machines crush, shear and draw in. Most injuries happen when someone reaches into the tools, bypasses a guard, or two people work one machine without clear control. As the person in charge, you check the safety devices, control who operates, and stop unsafe work at once.

head: Machine
Main hazards
Key controls
rows: Press brake
Crushing between punch and die; sheet whipping up as it bends; heavy tools falling
Light curtain or guards; two-hand control or guarded foot pedal; emergency stops; one operator in control; holding tools for small parts; stand clear of sheet whip
Box-and-pan or manual folder
Fingers trapped at the clamp beam; swinging apron; sharp edges
Hands clear when clamping; one person controls the apron; gloves for handling sheet
Plate bending rolls
Hands, gloves, sleeves and rags drawn into the **nip**; heavy plate falling or swinging
Trip bar and emergency stops tested before use; no loose clothing; gloves kept away from the nip if the Centre's rules say; long plates supported by a second person or a crane
Section and pipe benders
Trapping at the former; bar or pipe swinging round
Guards; stand outside the swing; support long lengths
Guillotine
Fingers under the blade or the hold-downs
Fixed guard; never reach under it; push sheets with another piece; **hold-downs** clamp the sheet before the blade cuts; **blade clearance** set for the thickness
Hot forming area
Burns, fire, gas
Tongs, heat-resistant gloves, tinted goggles; area cleared; extinguisher

ul: A **light curtain** stops the ram when something breaks its beams. If it keeps tripping, find out why (a sheet edge, a helper's hand, dirty lenses, poor alignment). Never switch it off, mute it or tape over a sensor.
A **two-hand control** needs both of the operator's hands on buttons before the ram moves, so neither hand can be in the tools.
Test the emergency stops at the start of each session.
Nobody bypasses a guard, whatever the reason. A guard that stops the work is reported and fixed, not removed.

blocks.p: Before changing tools, clearing a jam, adjusting rolls or cleaning, **isolate** the machine (switch off at the isolator), **lock** the isolator off with your own padlock, **tag** it, and check it cannot start. This is called **lockout**. Lower or support the ram and the tools so nothing can drop. Press brake tools are heavy: lift them with help or a lifting aid.

ul: **One person** controls the machine and decides when to bend. Helpers holding a large sheet keep their hands clear and stand where the sheet cannot whip up into them; the operator checks everyone is clear before every stroke.
Small parts are fed with a holding tool or magnet, with hands outside the guarded area, never by holding the very edge near the tool.
Check that the punch and die suit the thickness and that the force is within the rating of the machine and the tools.

blocks.note: When you supervise trainees, stop any unsafe act on the spot: reaching under a guillotine guard, a hand near the nip of the rolls, a guard switched off "to save time". Explain why, show the safe way, and watch them do it.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: How metal behaves when it is bent

blocks.h: Stretching, squeezing and the neutral axis

blocks.p: When metal is bent, the **outside** of the bend is stretched and gets slightly **thinner**, and the **inside** is squeezed. Somewhere in between is a layer that is neither stretched nor squeezed: the **neutral axis**. Its length does not change, so blank lengths are worked out along it.

ul: For gentle bends (a large inside radius) the neutral axis is near the middle of the thickness.
For tight bends it moves towards the inside. The **K-factor** gives where it lies, as a fraction of the thickness measured from the inside: often between about 0.33 and 0.5.

blocks.h: Elastic and plastic bending, and springback

blocks.p: Bend metal a little and it springs straight back (elastic). Bend it further and it stays bent (plastic). Even then, part of the bend is elastic, so when the force is taken off the part **springs back** a little and opens up.

head: Springback is greater when
Why
rows: The metal is stronger (stainless steel, high-strength steel)
More of the bend is elastic
The inside radius is larger, or the V-die wider
Less of the metal is bent fully plastic
The metal is thinner for the same radius
Same reason

blocks.p: The usual fix is to **overbend**: if a bend comes out at 92° when 90° is wanted, bend to about 88°. Bottoming or coining (see the press brake section) also reduces springback.

head: Material
How it bends
What to change
rows: Mild steel
Easiest; moderate force; can usually be bent cold to an inside radius about equal to its thickness; little springback
A small overbend
Stainless steel
Stronger and **work-hardens** as it bends; more springback; surface marks and steel particles cause rust spots later
More force (check the rating), more overbend, often a larger radius; clean tools kept for stainless, protective film
Aluminium
Soft, but some alloys and hard tempers crack if bent tightly; scratches easily
A larger inside radius as the maker's chart gives, or a softer temper; clean, smooth tools
High-strength steel
Strong; much springback; may crack at small radii
Follow the steel maker's minimum radius and the procedure

ul: **Grain direction**: rolled sheet and plate have a grain along the rolling direction. Bend **across** the grain (bend line at right angles to the rolling direction) wherever possible: bending along the grain is much more likely to crack on the outside.
Rough, burred cut edges at a bend start cracks: deburr them.
**Ductile** metals can be bent or stretched a long way without cracking.
Do not bend steel at a **blue heat** (roughly 200–400 °C, when it shows blue temper colours): it is more brittle then and can crack. Bend it cold, or hot at a full red heat.
After heavy cold forming, a part may be **stress relieved** (heated to a moderate temperature and cooled slowly) to reduce the stresses locked in by the forming.
**Normalising** (heating above the critical temperature and cooling in still air) refines the grain of steel after hot forming, when the specification asks for it.

blocks.p: The **bend allowance** is the length of the neutral axis through the bend. For a 90° bend it is a quarter of a circle:

head: Formula
Notes
rows: Neutral radius = inside radius + (K × thickness)
K = 0.5 puts it at mid-thickness
Bend allowance (90°) = 1.571 × neutral radius
Bend allowance (any angle) = 0.01745 × angle × neutral radius
Blank length = flat lengths + bend allowances
Flat lengths are measured to where each bend starts

head: Worked example
Working
rows: L-bracket in 2 mm sheet, inside radius 2 mm, outside sizes 40 mm and 25 mm, 90° bend, K = 0.5
Neutral radius = 2 + (0.5 × 2) = 3 mm
Bend allowance = 1.571 × 3 = 4.71 mm
Each flat = outside size − (inside radius + thickness) = outside size − 4 mm, so 36 mm and 21 mm

blocks.p: Many shops work from the **outside sizes** on the drawing. Add them up, then take away a **bend deduction** for each bend, taken from the shop's chart for its tools (or worked out: for 90°, bend deduction = 2 × (inside radius + thickness) − bend allowance).

head: Worked example
Working
rows: The same L-bracket: outside sizes 40 + 25 = 65 mm
Bend deduction = 2 × 4 − 4.71 = 3.29 mm; blank = 65 − 3.29 = **61.7 mm** (the same answer)
Channel 30 × 60 × 30 mm outside, bend deduction 3.5 mm per bend

blocks.note: Always prove the blank with a test bend before the batch. The chart or K-factor is a starting point; tooling, material and the real radius decide the final figure.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Rule (guide only: check the tooling chart)
Worked example
rows: V-die opening for air bending mild steel: about **8 × thickness**
2 mm sheet: about 16 mm; 4 mm: about 32 mm
Inside radius in air bending mild steel: roughly one-sixth of the V opening
16 mm die: about 2.7 mm
Force rises with the **square of the thickness**
Twice the thickness on the same die: 2² = 4 times the force
Force rises in step with the **length** of bend
A 2 m bend needs twice the force of a 1 m bend
Stronger material needs more force
Stainless steel often needs about half as much again as mild steel

head: Sum
Method
Worked example
rows: Cylinder blank length
Mean diameter × π, where mean diameter = outside diameter − thickness
Ring from flat bar rolled flat
Mean diameter × π, with the mean diameter at mid-thickness
Ring 300 mm inside diameter from 8 mm thick bar: mean diameter 308 mm; 308 × 3.142 = **967.7 mm**, plus a trim allowance
Arc length of a bent pipe or bar
0.01745 × angle × centre-line radius
Out-of-roundness (%)
(largest − smallest diameter) ÷ nominal diameter × 100

head: Sum
Worked example
rows: Steel sheet weighs about 7.85 kg per m² for each 1 mm of thickness
Parts in a day = (working time − set-up time) ÷ time per part
8 hours (480 min), 60 min set-up, 2 min a part: 420 ÷ 2 = **210 parts**

head: Method
How
Points
rows: Air bending
The punch pushes the sheet into the V-die, but the sheet **never touches the die floor**; it touches only the punch tip and the two die shoulders
The angle is set by **how deep the punch goes**. One die makes many angles; least force; springback must be allowed for
Bottoming
The punch presses the sheet down onto the die's sides
More accurate angle, less springback; more force; die angle must suit
Coining
Very high force presses the punch tip into the metal
Very accurate; needs several times the force of air bending; rarely used on thick work

blocks.p: In air bending, a **deeper** stroke gives a **smaller** (tighter) angle. If a bend comes out over-bent (for example 88.5° when 90° ± 1° is wanted), raise the stroke depth a little; if it is under-bent, go a little deeper. Make small changes and re-check.

ul: Choose a V-die opening to suit the thickness (about 8 × thickness for mild steel as a starting point), and a punch tip radius to suit the inside radius on the drawing.
A very sharp punch or too narrow a die gives too tight a radius, which can crack the outside of the bend.
Check the force from the machine's force chart is within the rating of the machine **and** of the tools, especially for stainless steel and thick plate.
Set the **back gauge** to give the flange length, and check it on the first part.

blocks.p: A flange must reach well across the V-die opening so the sheet is supported on both die shoulders as it bends. If it is too short, it drops into the die and the bend is not made properly. The tooling chart gives a minimum flange for each die (often roughly 0.7 × the V opening). The fix is a narrower die that still suits the thickness, or a design change agreed in writing.

Under load, the ram and bed of a press brake bend (deflect) slightly, most in the middle. A long part then comes out with a more open angle in the middle than at the ends (for example 90° at the ends and 92° in the middle). **Crowning** bows the bed or tools slightly to cancel this deflection, so the angle is the same all along.

Where a flange is bent up next to an edge that is not bent, the metal at the corner can tear. A small **relief cut** (a notch or slot at the end of the bend line, a little deeper than the bend radius plus the thickness) stops the tearing.

ul: A **box-and-pan folder** has a clamp beam made of removable fingers, so boxes and trays can be folded with the earlier sides fitting between the fingers.
A **hand folder** suits light sheet and short runs. Thick plate (for example 10 mm) is bent on a press brake, not a folder.
Allow for springback by folding slightly past the angle, and check with a protractor.

blocks.p: Most shop rolls have three rolls. On a **pinch-type** machine, the plate is gripped between two rolls and bent by the third, and the ends can be pre-bent on the machine. On a **pyramid-type** machine, one top roll sits above two bottom rolls; it cannot bend the very ends, so they are pre-bent on a press brake first.

flow: Work out the blank length from the **mean diameter** (mean diameter × π) and cut the blank **square**
Make a **template** to the outside radius from thin sheet or hardboard
Set the rolls **parallel** and adjust them for the thickness
**Pre-bend both ends**, so they curve like the rest of the shell
Feed the plate in square to the rolls; support long plates with a second person or a crane as they curve up
Roll a little at a time, checking with the template after each pass; stop before it is too tight (it is hard to open a shell up again)
Tack the seam with the edges level, at even spacing
Measure the diameter in several directions at each end and the middle; weld in a balanced way; check the shape again after welding

head: Fault
What it looks like
Likely cause
Prevention
rows: Peaking
A point at the seam instead of a smooth curve; a gap at the middle of the template held across the seam
Ends not pre-bent enough, so they stayed flat; weld shrinkage pulling the seam
Pre-bend both ends fully; balanced welding
Cone shape
One end a bigger diameter than the other
Rolls not parallel; plate fed in at an angle; blank not square
Set the rolls parallel; feed square; cut the blank square
Out of round
Diameters differ in different directions
Uneven rolling; over-rolling; flat ends
Small, even passes; template checks; pre-bend
Barrel or hourglass shape
Middle bigger or smaller than the ends
Rolls bending under load on long, thick plate
Lighter passes; machine within its capacity
Twisted seam (edges not level)
Edges overlap or step at the seam
Plate fed skew; blank not square
Feed square; check the blank

head: Section
Shape of the cross-section
Typical use
rows: Flat bar
A thin rectangle
Rings, brackets, gate frames
Angle
An L
Frames, supports, stiffeners
Channel
A squared-off C
Trailer chassis, frames, purlins
Beam (I-beam, universal beam or column)
A capital I or H: two flanges joined by a web
Building frames, columns, crane runways
Hollow sections (square, rectangular, round)
A closed tube
Handrails, columns, gates, trusses
Round and square bar
Solid round or square
Hooks, scrolls, pins, grilles

ul: Work out the length along the neutral axis: for flat bar rolled flat, the mean diameter × π. For angle and other sections, use the shop's chart. Add an allowance to trim.
Roll on section rolls or bend round a former in small steps, checking with a template.
**Angle rolled "leg in"**: the leg on the inside of the curve is squeezed and can buckle or wave. **"Leg out"**: that leg is stretched and can thin or crack if the radius is tight.
Bars twist as they are rolled: set the guide rolls to hold the section upright, and check for twist on a flat table.

sections.title: Pipe, tube and section bending, and hot forming

ul: Bent too tightly, a pipe **wrinkles on the inside** of the bend, goes **oval**, and thins on the outside. Use the former (die) that fits the pipe size and gives the radius on the drawing.
Thin-walled tube bent to a tight radius needs a **mandrel** (an inside support) to stop it flattening and wrinkling.
As a rough guide, many pipes bend cold without a mandrel to a centre-line radius of about 3–5 times the outside diameter; tighter bends need the right tooling. Follow the bender maker's chart.
On welded tube, put the weld seam at the **side** of the bend (on the neutral axis), not on the inside or the outside, where it would be squeezed or stretched and may split.
The length of pipe in a bend is the arc length along the centre line: 0.01745 × angle × centre-line radius.

blocks.p: To bend angle iron to a corner, cut a **V-notch** out of the leg that lies across the bend, bend the other leg sharply at the notch, then weld the closed notch. The notch angle is **180° minus the corner angle**: 90° for a square corner, 120° for a 60° corner. Mark the notch from the heel of the angle so the outside sizes come out right.
Thick bar and sections that are too stiff to bend cold, or must be bent to a tight radius, are heated first. Hammering or pressing hot steel into shape, as a blacksmith does, is called **forging**.

head: Colour of mild steel (in shade)
Rough temperature
Use
rows: Black heat (no glow), but hot
Below about 450 °C
Too cold to hot bend; blue heat (about 200–400 °C) is a brittle range: do not bend
Dull red
About 600–700 °C
Upper limit for flame straightening; too cool for heavy bending
Even bright red to light cherry red
About 850–950 °C
Hot bending and forming
Yellow to white with sparks, surface bubbling
Well over 1 200 °C
**Burnt**: the steel is spoiled and must be scrapped

flow: Read the drawing; mark bend positions with a **centre punch** (soapstone burns off); make a template or jig
Set up a safe area: anything that burns cleared, a heavy vice or bending fork, tongs, an extinguisher; check the gas set
Wear tinted goggles, heat-resistant gloves, flame-resistant clothing and boots
Heat evenly all round the bar and over the full length of the bend, to an even bright red
Bend steadily; check against the template; reheat if it cools to a dull or blue heat
Check that each bend is in the right plane and position
Let it cool slowly in **still air**; mark it HOT; never throw it in water
Clean off the **scale** (the hard, flaky oxide) and check against the drawing

blocks.note: Fast, uneven cooling in water can distort and crack a hot-formed part, and on higher-carbon steel it can make it hard and brittle. Cool in still air unless the procedure says otherwise.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Check
Tool
rows: Bend angle
Protractor (bevel protractor) or angle gauge
Inside radius
Radius gauge
Flange lengths, hole positions
Steel rule, tape or vernier caliper
Squareness
Engineer's square
Flatness and twist
Straight edge or flat table, with feeler gauges
Curvature of a rolled shell
Template; diameters with large calipers or a circumference tape
Surface
By eye in good light: cracks on the outside of bends, tool marks, scratches, dents

ul: Check the first-off fully, then a sample at set intervals, or every part if the drawing or customer asks.
Compare each reading with the tolerance. For example, with 90° ± 1°, angles from 89° to 91° pass; 88.5° or 91.5° fail.
Record results on an inspection sheet: part number, measurements, pass or fail, date, name.
Give a failed part a **reject tag** and keep it apart so it cannot be mixed with good parts.

head: Problem
Check first
rows: Flanges short or long on a batch
Blank sizes and the back gauge setting, before changing anything else
Angles vary along a long bend
Machine deflection and crowning; tool wear
Angles vary from part to part
Material thickness and grade differences; back gauge; stroke depth
Cracks on the outside of bends
Radius tighter than allowed; bending along the grain; burred edges; wrong grade or temper; worn or sharp tooling

flow: Stop the batch and quarantine all the parts, good and bad
Count and record how many are affected and where the fault is
Check the drawing, the material certificate, the tooling and the settings
Prove the cause with test bends
Report: the job, number affected, what you found, the cause, what was done with the parts, and recommendations
Put the fix in place and check the next parts

blocks.p: When the batch is finished, record the quantity, the blank size, the tooling and settings, the first-off result, the checks made and their results, and any rejects and their cause. This lets the job be repeated right first time.
Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section.

ul: I can read a drawing and process sheet and plan a forming job, including the bending order and a first-off.
I can check the guards, light curtain, two-hand control and emergency stops, and lock off a machine.
I can control sheet whip, nip points and small-part feeding, and supervise others on forming machines.
I can explain the neutral axis, K-factor, springback, thinning, work hardening and grain direction.
I can explain why steel must not be bent at a blue heat, and what stress relieving and normalising do.
I can work out bend allowance, bend deduction and blank lengths.
I can choose a V-die opening and estimate how force changes with thickness, length and material.
I can explain air bending, bottoming, coining, crowning and relief cuts.
I can work out cylinder and ring blank lengths, arc lengths and out-of-roundness.
I can roll a cylinder with pre-bent ends and template checks, and explain peaking and coning.
I can bend pipe without wrinkling, and notch angle for a corner.
I can hot form bar safely, at the right heat, and cool it correctly.
I can inspect formed parts with the right tools, tag rejects and investigate faults.
I can work out weights and output, and complete the job card.

terms: Air bending
Bending in a V-die without the sheet touching the die floor; the stroke depth sets the angle
Back gauge
The adjustable stop behind the tools that sets the flange length
Bend allowance
The length of the neutral axis through a bend
Bend deduction
The amount taken off the sum of the outside sizes for each bend
Blade clearance
The gap between a guillotine's blades, set to the thickness
Blank
The flat piece cut to size before forming
Bottoming
Pressing the sheet onto the sides of the die to set the angle
Crowning
Bowing the bed or tools slightly so a long bend has the same angle all along
Ductile
Able to bend or stretch a long way without cracking
First-off
The first part made, fully checked before the batch
Forging
Hammering or pressing hot metal into shape
Hold-down
The clamps on a guillotine that hold the sheet before the blade cuts
K-factor
Where the neutral axis lies, as a fraction of the thickness from the inside
Lockout
Isolating a machine, locking the isolator and tagging it before work on it
Mandrel
An inside support that stops tube flattening and wrinkling as it bends
Mean diameter
The diameter at mid-thickness: outside diameter minus the thickness
Neutral axis
The layer in a bend that is neither stretched nor squeezed
Normalising
Heating steel above its critical temperature and cooling in still air to refine the grain
Peaking
A point at the seam of a rolled cylinder, caused by flat ends
Pre-bending
Bending the ends of a plate before rolling so they curve like the rest
Relief cut
A small notch at the end of a bend line to stop tearing
Scale
The hard, flaky oxide on heated steel
Springback
The partial opening of a bend when the force is removed
Two-hand control
A control that needs both hands on buttons before the machine moves

c1.title: Cable-tray brackets in Williamsfield
c1.text: Jodi-Ann leads a team making 120 L-shaped brackets for cable trays at a shop in Williamsfield, Manchester. The brackets are 3 mm mild steel, with outside sizes of 60 mm and 40 mm, a 3 mm inside radius, and a 90° ± 1° bend. The team uses a 24 mm V-die and takes the neutral axis at mid-thickness (K = 0.5). The first-off bracket measures 88.4°. A second part on the job has a flange only 10 mm long. Setting up takes about 45 minutes, and each bracket then takes about 1.5 minutes.

c2.title: A tank shell in Seaforth
c2.text: Garth is rolling a short shell for a water tank at a shop in Seaforth, St Thomas, from 5 mm mild steel plate. The drawing gives an outside diameter of 600 mm and allows an out-of-roundness of 1% of the diameter. After tacking, he measures 606 mm one way and 593 mm the other. A template held across the seam shows a gap at its middle, with a point at the seam.

c3.title: Handrails for a school in Constant Spring
c3.text: A team is bending 42.4 mm outside diameter welded steel tube for handrails at a school in Constant Spring, St Andrew, on a hand bender. The drawing gives 45° bends on a 160 mm centre-line radius. A trainee used a smaller former he found on the bench, and his bends have wrinkled on the inside and gone oval. Some of the trainees' bends have also split along the tube's weld seam.

c4.title: Gate scrolls and a frame in Bath
c4.text: At a workshop in Bath, St Thomas, Wayne is hot forming 20 mm square bar into scrolls for a gate. A trainee heats one bar until it throws bright sparks and its surface bubbles. Another trainee keeps bending a bar after its glow has gone and it shows blue colours. The job also needs a triangular frame of 50 mm angle with 60° corners, and a ring of 40 mm × 6 mm flat bar, rolled flat, with an outside diameter of 500 mm.

c5.title: The press brake team in Little London
c5.text: Nadine supervises trainees on a 40-tonne press brake at a centre in Little London, Westmoreland. One trainee holds a large sheet while another works the foot pedal, and they talk to each other about when to bend. The force chart gives about 22 tonnes per metre for 3 mm mild steel on the 24 mm die, and notes that stainless steel needs about 1.5 times as much. The next job is a 1.5 m long bend in 3 mm stainless steel. Some aluminium cover plates bent last week cracked along the outside of their bends; the bend lines ran along the rolling direction.

questions.q: How long must the team cut each flat piece before it is bent?
questions.why: Each flat is the outside size less (radius + thickness): 54 and 34 mm. The neutral radius is 3 + 1.5 = 4.5 mm, so the bend allowance is 1.571 × 4.5 = 7.07 mm. Blank = 54 + 34 + 7.07 = 95.1 mm.

questions.q: The first-off is 88.4°. What should Jodi-Ann change?
o: Nothing: 88.4° is close enough to 90° for a bracket
Make the punch go deeper so the angle comes out tighter
Make the stroke a little shallower, then check again
Move the back gauge further away from the bend line
questions.why: The tolerance is 89° to 91°, so 88.4° fails: the bend is over-bent. In air bending the stroke depth sets the angle; a slightly shallower stroke opens it up. Change a little, bend another first-off and re-measure.

questions.q: The 10 mm flange will not bend properly on the 24 mm die. What is the best fix?
o: Use a narrower die that the chart allows for 3 mm
Press harder so the flange is forced round the die
Hold the flange down on the die by hand as it bends
Heat the flange so it bends more easily on the die
questions.why: A flange must reach well across the V opening to be supported on both shoulders. A narrower die that still suits 3 mm sheet, or a design change agreed in writing, solves it. Holding sheet by hand near the tools is never safe.

questions.q: About how long will the batch of 120 brackets take, including set-up?
o: 2 hours 15 minutes
3 hours
3 hours 45 minutes
4 hours 30 minutes
questions.why: Bending: 120 × 1.5 = 180 minutes. Add 45 minutes of set-up: 225 minutes, or 3 hours 45 minutes.

questions.q: What blank length should Garth have cut for the shell?
o: About 1 885 mm
About 1 870 mm
About 1 854 mm
About 1 900 mm
questions.why: Use the mean diameter, at mid-thickness: 600 − 5 = 595 mm. Blank = 595 × 3.142 = about 1 869.5 mm. Using the outside diameter (600 × 3.142 = 1 885 mm) makes the shell too big.

questions.q: Is the shell within its out-of-roundness limit?
o: Yes: the average of the two readings is close to 600 mm
Yes: 13 mm is under the 1% that 600 mm allows
No: it is about 2.2% out, over the 1% limit
No: any difference at all in the diameter fails
questions.why: Out-of-roundness = (606 − 593) ÷ 600 × 100 = 13 ÷ 600 × 100 ≈ 2.2%. The limit is 1%, which is 6 mm on 600 mm, so the shell fails and must be reworked.

questions.q: What most likely caused the point at the seam, and how is it prevented next time?
o: Rolls not parallel: set them parallel before rolling
Plate too long: cut the blank from the outside diameter
Rolled too slowly: feed the plate through faster
Ends left flat: pre-bend both ends before rolling
questions.why: Rolls cannot curve the very ends of a plate, so ends that are not pre-bent stay flat and meet in a point. Pre-bend both ends fully, roll in small steps with the template, and weld in a balanced way.

questions.q: Why did the trainee's bends wrinkle and go oval?
o: Too small a former for the tube and the radius
The tube was bent too slowly on the hand bender
The tube was too thick-walled for any bending
The bends should have been made at 90°, not 45°
questions.why: Bent too tightly, the inside of a tube is squeezed into wrinkles and the tube flattens. Use the former made for 42.4 mm tube at the drawing's radius; tighter bends need a mandrel.

questions.q: About how long, along the centre line, is each 45° bend?
o: About 63 mm
About 126 mm
About 251 mm
About 1 005 mm
questions.why: Arc length = 0.01745 × angle × radius = 0.01745 × 45 × 160 ≈ 125.6 mm. A whole circle at that radius would be 2 × 3.142 × 160 ≈ 1 005 mm, and 45° is one-eighth of it.

questions.q: Where should the tube's weld seam be placed in the bender?
o: On the outside of the bend, where it is easy to see
On the inside of the bend, where it is squeezed tight
Anywhere, as the seam is as strong as the tube
At the side of the bend, on the neutral axis
questions.why: The outside of a bend stretches and the inside is squeezed. At the side the seam sits near the neutral axis, where it is neither stretched nor squeezed, so it is least likely to split.

questions.q: What should happen to the bar that threw bright sparks with a bubbling surface?
o: Bend it at once while it is at its best heat
Quench it in water to harden the surface again
Scrap it: the steel is burnt and spoiled
Let it cool a little and then bend it as planned
questions.why: Sparks and a bubbling surface mean the steel is burnt: it has started to oxidise inside and is weak and brittle. It cannot be saved. Hot bending is done at an even bright red.

questions.q: Why is it wrong to keep bending the bar once it shows blue colours?
o: Steel at a blue heat is more brittle and may crack
The blue scale will stick to the tools and mark them
It is too soft at a blue heat to keep its shape
Blue steel has turned into a spring and will not stay bent
questions.why: In the blue-heat range (roughly 200–400 °C) steel is less ductile and can crack if it is bent. Reheat it to bright red, or bend it fully cold if the section allows.

questions.q: What notch angle is cut in the angle for each 60° corner of the frame?
questions.why: The notch is 180° minus the corner angle: 180 − 60 = 120°. When the other leg is bent, the notch closes and is welded. A square corner needs a 90° notch.

questions.q: What length of flat bar is needed for the ring, before any trim allowance?
o: About 1 571 mm
About 1 552 mm
About 1 533 mm
About 1 590 mm
questions.why: For bar rolled flat, measure along the mid-thickness: mean diameter = 500 − 6 = 494 mm. Length = 494 × 3.142 ≈ 1 552 mm. Using the outside diameter gives about 1 571 mm, too long.

questions.q: What should Nadine change about how the two trainees work the press brake?
o: Let the one holding the sheet call out when to bend
Have the pedal pressed only when both shout "clear"
One operator controls it and checks all are clear
Let them take turns on the pedal after every bend
questions.why: When two people share control by talking, one can bend while the other's hands are still near the tools. One operator controls the machine, checks everyone is clear before each stroke, and helpers keep their hands outside the guarded area.

questions.q: Can the 40-tonne press brake make the 1.5 m bend in stainless steel?
o: Yes: it needs about 33 tonnes
Yes: it needs about 22 tonnes
No: it needs about 74 tonnes
No: it needs about 49.5 tonnes
questions.why: Force per metre for stainless: 22 × 1.5 = 33 t. For 1.5 m: 33 × 1.5 = 49.5 t, more than the 40 t rating. Use a wider die the chart allows, a bigger machine, or shorter bends, and check the tools' rating too.

questions.q: What is the most likely reason the aluminium cover plates cracked?
o: Bent along the grain at too tight a radius
They were bent too slowly on the press brake
The V-die was much too wide for the sheet
The sheet had protective film on its surface
questions.why: Bending with the bend line along the rolling direction makes the outside of the bend much more likely to crack, especially at a tight radius or in a hard temper. Bend across the grain, use the radius the maker gives, or choose a softer temper.

questions.q: About how much does a 2.4 m × 1.2 m sheet of 4 mm steel weigh?
o: About 23 kg
About 90 kg
About 9 kg
About 226 kg
questions.why: Area = 2.4 × 1.2 = 2.88 m². Weight = 2.88 × 4 × 7.85 ≈ 90 kg. That is too heavy for one person: use two people or a lifting aid.

questions.q: Why are blanks laid out so the bend lines run across the sheet's rolling direction?
o: The sheet is softer that way, so less force is needed
Bends across the grain are less likely to crack
It makes the blank length calculation simpler
The springback is removed completely that way
questions.why: The rolling direction gives sheet a grain. Bending along it puts the stretched outside of the bend on the weakest direction, so it cracks more easily, especially at tight radii.

questions.q: A shop chart puts the neutral axis at K = 0.4 for tight bends, not 0.5. Compared with a sum using 0.5, what does this do to the blank length?
o: Makes it a little longer
Makes it about twice as long
Makes it a little shorter
Leaves it exactly the same
questions.why: A smaller K-factor puts the neutral axis nearer the inside, so its radius and the bend allowance are smaller, and the blank comes out a little shorter. A test bend confirms the figure.
